The Judicial Branch. The system of federal courts, headed by the Supreme Court, that interprets and applies the law and reviews whether government actions comply with the Constitution. One of the three coordinate powers in the separation of powers framework, it can strike down laws and executive actions deemed unconstitutional. The judiciary's power of judicial review, though not explicitly mentioned in the Constitution, grew from Marbury v. Madison in 1803 and became central to American governance.

The Judicial Branch consists of the Supreme Court, federal courts of appeals, and district courts, creating a hierarchy of judicial authority. The Supreme Court has nine justices appointed for life; lower federal judges also serve for life, insulating them from political pressure. This branch exercises judicial review—the power to invalidate laws or government actions it deems unconstitutional, a practice established in Marbury v. Madison. The Judicial Branch is subject to checks: Congress can propose constitutional amendments, impeach judges, set the Court's size, and define its jurisdiction; the President appoints justices with Senate confirmation. The courts interpret the Constitution and federal statutes, mediating disputes between individuals and government, and between federal and state power. Major Court decisions like Plessy v. Ferguson, Brown v. Board of Education, and Roe v. Wade have reshaped American society on race, education, and rights. Federal judges are appointed for life to protect judicial independence from political pressure, though this also creates accountability questions when judges remain on the bench for decades. The Supreme Court's ability to overturn laws and presidential actions makes it a powerful co-equal branch; appointments of new justices can shift jurisprudence for generations to come. The Judicial Branch's power grows from and is constrained by the Constitution, the system of checks and balances that bind it to the legislative and executive branches.
